claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies and represents established knowledge.

claims.claim: GWAS studies have identified thousands of variants associated with various blood cell traits.
claims.source: In the context of hematopoiesis, GWAS studies have identified thousands of variants associated with various blood cell traits, including hundreds associated with red blood cell traits alone (Astle et al., 2016; van der Harst et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to published GWAS studies.

claims.claim: BCL11A is a key regulator of fetal hemoglobin expression.
claims.source: Thorough follow-up efforts at individual loci have identified important regulators of hematopoiesis, such as the key regulator of fetal hemoglobin expression, BCL11A (Basak et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2018; Sankaran et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claims.claim: The study focused on 75 loci associated with RBC traits identified by a GWAS performed in up to 135,000 individuals.
claims.source: We focused on 75 loci associated with RBC traits that were identified by a GWAS performed in up to 135,000 individuals (van der Harst et al., 2012) spanning 6 RBC traits (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This describes the source of the loci used in the study, supported by citation.

claims.claim: The 75 loci have been robustly replicated in more recently reported association studies performed on larger cohorts.
claims.source: Importantly, these 75 loci have been robustly replicated in more recently reported association studies performed on larger cohorts and thus represent important targets for perturbation studies (Astle et al., 2016; Ulirsch et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to more recent GWAS studies.

claims.claim: Each of the 75 sentinel SNPs was expanded to a linkage disequilibrium (LD) block including all SNPs in high LD (r2 >0.8).
claims.source: To do this, each of the 75 sentinel SNPs was first expanded to a linkage disequilibrium (LD) block including all SNPs in high LD (r2 >0.8, Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), then further to the nearest genomic recombination hotspot.
claims.evidence: This describes the computational method used to define genomic regions.

claims.claim: Each gene was expanded to include a wingspan encompassing 110 kb upstream and 40 kb downstream of the transcriptional start and end sites.
claims.source: Based upon insights from previous expression quantitative trait locus (eQTL) studies (Montgomery and Dermitzakis, 2011; International Inflammatory Bowel Disease Genetics Constortium et al., 2011; Veyrieras et al., 2008), each gene annotated in the genome was expanded to include a wingspan encompassing 110 kb upstream and 40 kb downstream of the transcriptional start and end sites, respectively, to also capture potential functional regulatory elements.
claims.evidence: This describes the method used to define gene regions, informed by cited eQTL studies.

claims.claim: 389 genes overlapping or in the vicinity of the LD blocks were selected to be tested in the pooled loss-of-function screen.
claims.source: This resulted in selection of 389 genes overlapping or in the vicinity of the LD blocks to be tested in the pooled loss-of-function screen.
claims.evidence: This describes the outcome of the gene selection process.

claims.claim: The genes were distributed at a median of 4 genes per loci.
claims.source: These were distributed at a median of 4 genes per loci (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the gene selection process, shown in a figure.

claims.claim: The approach may miss genes targeted by a trait-associated regulatory element in cases of long-range interactions.
claims.source: This approach may on occasion miss genes targeted by a trait-associated regulatory element. For example, our approach would miss long-range interactions, as is observed at the FTO locus with IRX3/IRX5 (Claussnitzer et al., 2015; Smemo et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is an acknowledged limitation of the method, supported by citations to examples.

claims.claim: LD and related metrics will only nominate a fraction of potential regulatory targets.
claims.source: It is becoming increasingly clear that LD and related metrics will only nominate a fraction of potential regulatory targets (Whalen and Pollard, 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to published work.

claims.claim: The majority of common genetic variation underlying RBC traits appears to act in a cell-intrinsic manner within the erythroid lineage.
claims.source: Since the majority of common genetic variation underlying RBC traits appears to act in a cell-intrinsic manner within the erythroid lineage, we decided to perturb the candidate genes during the process of human erythropoiesis (Giani et al., 2016; Sankaran et al., 2012; Sankaran et al., 2008; Ulirsch et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claims.claim: shRNA-based approaches in primary CD34+ HSPC-derived erythroid cells have been successful in validating individual genes underlying RBC traits.
claims.source: First, we have had prior success validating individual genes underlying RBC traits using shRNA-based approaches in primary CD34+ HSPC-derived erythroid cells and our results have been consistent with orthogonal CRISPR based approaches (Giani et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work from the authors.

claims.claim: shRNA libraries can be much more efficiently packaged into lentiviruses and delivered to primary HSPCs compared to alternative CRISPR/Cas9-based guide RNA libraries.
claims.source: Second, shRNA libraries can be much more efficiently packaged into lentiviruses and delivered to primary HSPCs compared to alternative CRISPR/Cas9-based guide RNA libraries (Ting et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation and represents a technical consideration.

claims.claim: All-in-one CRISPR or CRISPRi lentiviral constructs produce low titer viruses and require very high multiplicities of infection.
claims.source: We observe that all in one CRISPR or CRISPRi lentiviral constructs that are ideal for primary HSPC screens produce low titer viruses and require very high multiplicities of infection that can be challenging to achieve for a pooled functional screen (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the authors' experiments shown in a figure.

claims.claim: CRISPR/Cas9 based approaches can produce non-uniform loss-of-function or gain-of-function outcomes due to unpredictable DNA repair processes.
claims.source: Third, the shRNA approach avoids potential complications like non-uniform loss-of-function or gain-of-function outcomes produced by CRISPR/Cas9 based approaches due to unpredictable DNA repair processes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C) (Mandegar et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation and data shown in a figure.

claims.claim: shRNAs can act rapidly to achieve gene knockdown and thereby avoid compensatory effects that can occur when complete CRISPR knockout is achieved.
claims.source: Furthermore, shRNAs can act rapidly to achieve gene knockdown and thereby avoid compensatory effects that can occur when complete CRISPR knockout is achieved (Rossi et al., 2015), better recapitulating the subtle changes in gene expression that are characteristic of common genetic variation.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation and represents a theoretical advantage.

claims.claim: The pooled shRNA library consisted of 2803 hairpins targeting the 389 GWAS-nominated genes, along with 30 control genes.
claims.source: Mobilized peripheral blood-derived primary human CD34+ HSPCs from three independent healthy donors were infected with a lentiviral-based pooled shRNA library consisting of 2803 hairpins targeting the 389 GWAS-nominated genes, along with 30 control genes (Moffat et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This describes the composition of the experimental library.

claims.claim: Each GWAS-nominated gene was targeted with 5-7 distinct shRNAs.
claims.source: Each GWAS-nominated gene was targeted with 5–7 distinct shRNAs (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental design, shown in a figure.

claims.claim: An infectivity of 35-50% was achieved.
claims.source: Using lentiviral libraries with defined titers, we achieved an infectivity of 35–50%, which provides a good tradeoff between reasonably high infection while minimizing the possibility of multiple integrations per cell that can lead to combinatorial phenotypes.
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation.

claims.claim: At least 1000 CD34+ HSPCs per hairpin were infected (7 ~ 11 * 10^6 cells per experiment).
claims.source: To achieve sufficient library representation, we infected at least 1000 CD34+ HSPCs per hairpin (7 ~ 11 * 106 cells per experiment).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental scale.

claims.claim: Hairpins targeting potential regulators of erythropoiesis would be depleted or enriched during the three-phase erythroid culture.
claims.source: We hypothesized that hairpins targeting potential regulators of erythropoiesis would be depleted or enriched during the three-phase erythroid culture, similar to our prior experience in analyzing specific GWAS-nominated genes (Giani et al., 2016; Sankaran et al., 2012; Ulirsch et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is the hypothesis of the study, informed by prior work cited.

claims.claim: Genomic DNA was isolated and deep-sequenced from the pool of infected cells at six different culture time points.
claims.source: To assay these hairpins, we isolated and deep-sequenced genomic DNA from the pool of infected cells at six different culture time points that represent distinct stages of erythropoiesis to most broadly assess putative causal genes that may act across the span of differentiation (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental method.

claims.claim: Greater than 95% of hairpins were represented at levels of at least five log2 counts per million (CPM) at day 4.
claims.source: Greater than 95% of hairpins were represented at levels of at least five log2 counts per million (CPM) at day 4, two days post-infection (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the sequencing data shown in a figure.

claims.claim: A diversity of effects - in terms of both increased and decreased hairpin abundance - were observed across the two-week time course.
claims.source: Across the two-week time course, a diversity of effects - in terms of both increased and decreased hairpin abundance - were observed.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claims.claim: Hairpins targeting genes with known biological roles in erythropoiesis, such as GATA1 and RPS19, showed markedly decreased abundance across the time course.
claims.source: Hairpins targeting genes with known biological roles in erythropoiesis, such as GATA1 and RPS19 (Khajuria et al., 2018; Ludwig et al., 2014), showed markedly decreased abundance across the time course.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data, with citations supporting the known roles of these genes.

claims.claim: Hairpins targeting a set of broadly essential genes were strongly depleted by day 16 when compared to negative control hairpins.
claims.source: Likewise, hairpins targeting a set of broadly essential genes (Figure 1—source data 2) were strongly depleted by day 16 when compared to negative control hairpins targeting non-human genes, which showed little if any change (Figure 2C–E).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in figures.

claims.claim: The trends were recapitulated with strong correlation in each of the three donor CD34+ cell backgrounds.
claims.source: These trends were recapitulated with strong correlation in each of the three donor CD34+ cell backgrounds (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is an observation about reproducibility across replicates, shown in a figure.

claims.claim: A linear mixed model was implemented to account for the longitudinal nature of the time course data.
claims.source: A linear mixed model was implemented to account for the longitudinal nature of the time course data (Li et al., 2015) and to handle the confounding off-target and efficiency effects inherent to the shRNA modality (Riba et al., 2017; Tsherniak et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This describes the statistical method used, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Absolute hairpin abundances at each time point were converted to a log2 fold change relative to the initial hairpin abundances at the start of the differentiation.
claims.source: Since we wanted our model to be able to detect significant changes in hairpin abundance at any time point throughout the differentiation process, we converted the absolute hairpin abundances at each of the six time points to a log2 fold change relative to the initial hairpin abundances at the start of the differentiation.
claims.evidence: This describes the data transformation used in the analysis.

claims.claim: Genes were called as hits if they had a fitted slope >0.1 log2 fold change per day within the interval while simultaneously possessing a Wald chi-square FDR-adjusted q value < 0.1.
claims.source: Specifically, genes were called as hits if they had a fitted slope >0.1 log2 fold change per day within the interval while simultaneously possessing a Wald chi-square FDR-adjusted q value < 0.1.
claims.evidence: This describes the statistical criteria for calling hits.

claims.claim: This approach identified 77 genes at 38 of the 75 targeted loci which, when suppressed, had a significant effect on the slope of shRNA-encoding DNA abundance at any point during the time course.
claims.source: In total, this approach identified 77 genes at 38 of the 75 targeted loci which, when suppressed, had a significant effect on the slope of shRNA-encoding DNA abundance at any point during the time course.
claims.evidence: This is the primary result of the statistical analysis.

claims.claim: A majority of the hit loci (27 loci) had 1-2 gene targets prioritized.
claims.source: A majority of these hit loci (27 loci) had 1–2 gene targets prioritized (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the results, shown in figures.

claims.claim: The candidate genes were found to be distributed across all 6 of the originally annotated RBC GWAS traits.
claims.source: These candidate genes were found to be distributed across all 6 of the originally annotated RBC GWAS traits (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B)
claims.evidence: This is an observation about the distribution of hits, shown in a figure.

claims.claim: Hairpins targeting the hit genes showed strong internal consistency.
claims.source: and hairpins targeting them showed strong internal consistency (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is an observation about the quality of the hits, shown in a figure.

claims.claim: The hit set was enriched for erythroid essentiality as quantified in the K562 erythroid cell line.
claims.source: A permutation comparing the sum of K562 essentiality scores for the hit genes with those of randomly drawn, identically-sized gene sets from the library of targeted genes revealed that the hit set was indeed enriched with p=0.0269 (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is a validation finding using permutation analysis and external data.

claims.claim: When compared to permuted sets of 77 genes randomly chosen from the genome, there was even stronger enrichment for erythroid essentiality with p=0.00021.
claims.source: Likewise, when compared to permuted sets of 77 genes randomly chosen from the genome (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A), there was even stronger enrichment for erythroid essentiality with p=0.00021
claims.evidence: This is a validation finding using permutation analysis.

claims.claim: The hit set was significantly enriched when compared to genes from libraries nominated by SNPs associated with lipid levels.
claims.source: We further explored whether the enrichment could be due to an intrinsic bias inherent to GWAS screening itself by permuting sets of genes from libraries nominated by SNPs associated with low-density lipoprotein levels, high-density lipoprotein levels, and triglyceride levels, finding the hit set to be significantly enriched in all comparisons (Global Lipids Genetics Consortium et al., 2013) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B–D).
claims.evidence: This is a validation finding using permutation analysis with external GWAS data.

claims.claim: Five 'gold standard' genes in the library possess known genetic underpinnings via identified causal variants: CCND3, SH2B3, MYB, KIT, and RBM38.
claims.source: We further validated the ability of this approach to discover genetically relevant hits by performing a permutation analysis based upon five 'gold standard' genes in the library, which possess known genetic underpinnings via identified causal variants: CCND3 (Sankaran et al., 2012; Ulirsch et al., 2019), SH2B3 (Giani et al., 2016), MYB (Galarneau et al., 2010; Sankaran et al., 2013; Sankaran et al., 2011), KIT (Jing et al., 2008; Ulirsch et al., 2019), and RBM38 (Ulirsch et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies for each gene.

claims.claim: Enrichment for the five gold standards was seen with p=0.0249.
claims.source: Calculating the rank sums of hairpins ordered by our model's computed FDR scores for 1,000,000 random combinations of five genes from the library yielded a distribution over which enrichment for the five gold standards was seen with p=0.0249 (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is a validation finding using permutation analysis.

claims.claim: Among the 389 GWAS-nominated genes in the library, 20 (~5%) were found to contain at least one coding variant with a minimum posterior probability of association of 0.1.
claims.source: Among the 389 GWAS-nominated genes in our library, 20 (~5%) were found to contain at least one coding variant from this list.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative observation from analysis of fine-mapped variants.

claims.claim: There was a significant enrichment of coding variants observed among the hits (~9%, p=0.03907).
claims.source: Of these, there was a significant enrichment observed among the hits (~9%, p=0.03907 as determined by permutation analysis; Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This is a validation finding using permutation analysis.

claims.claim: Common myeloid progenitors (CMPs) and megakaryocyte-erythroid progenitors (MEPs) were significantly enriched for hit gene expression (p<0.01).
claims.source: In the more holistic hematopoiesis dataset, common myeloid progenitors (CMPs) and megakaryocyte-erythroid progenitors (MEPs) were significantly enriched for hit gene expression (p<0.01).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from expression analysis using external datasets.

claims.claim: Proerythroblast, early basophilic, and late basophilic erythroblast stages were particularly enriched for hit gene expression (p<0.001).
claims.source: Within a more detailed and separate analysis of human adult erythropoiesis, proerythroblast, early basophilic, and late basophilic erythroblast stages were particularly enriched (p<0.001).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from expression analysis using external datasets.

claims.claim: None of the 77 shRNA screen hits emerged using eQTLs located within the LD blocks of the original 75 sentinel SNPs from the GTEx whole blood dataset.
claims.source: To examine how our results compare to target gene identification through eQTL-based approaches, we also examined the whole blood eQTL dataset form the Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx) Project, finding that none of the 77 shRNA screen hits emerged using eQTLs located within the LD blocks of the original 75 sentinel SNPs (GTEx Consortium, 2015).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison with external eQTL data.

claims.claim: The shRNA screen was performed on differentiating erythroid progenitors which are essentially not present in whole blood.
claims.source: This is not entirely surprising given that the shRNA screen was performed on differentiating erythroid progenitors which are essentially not present in whole blood, so one would expect to miss cell type-specific effects or eQTLs that act in early progenitor populations.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about why the eQTL comparison showed no overlap.

claims.claim: STRING interaction network analyses identified underlying networks between hits in the screen.
claims.source: Using STRING interaction network analyses (version 10.5) (Szklarczyk et al., 2017), we used empirical, database-curated, co-expression, genomic proximity, and text-mined evidence to identify underlying networks between hits in the screen.
claims.evidence: This describes the network analysis method used, supported by citation.

claims.claim: The networks highlighted interacting biological processes including cell signaling and transcription, cytoskeletal and membrane structure and function, and mRNA translation.
claims.source: These networks highlighted a number of interacting biological processes of both known and previously unappreciated importance to erythropoiesis (Figure 4), including cell signaling and transcription, cytoskeletal and membrane structure and function, and mRNA translation.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from network analysis shown in a figure.

claims.claim: MYB is a master regulator transcription factor that has been implicated in playing a role in fetal hemoglobin regulation and in erythropoiesis more generally.
claims.source: MYB is a master regulator transcription factor that has been implicated in playing a role in fetal hemoglobin regulation and in erythropoiesis more generally (Mucenski et al., 1991; Wang et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claims.claim: The MYB locus has been associated with numerous red blood cell traits.
claims.source: The MYB locus has been associated with numerous red blood cell traits (including mean corpuscular volume, mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration, and RBC count) (Sankaran et al., 2013; van der Harst et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to GWAS studies.

claims.claim: ETO2 (CBFA2T3) is a part of the erythroid transcription factor complex containing TAL1 and is required for expansion of erythroid progenitors.
claims.source: ETO2 (CBFA2T3) is a part of the erythroid transcription factor complex containing TAL1 and is required for expansion of erythroid progenitors (Goardon et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a published study.

claims.claim: Stem cell factor receptor KIT and erythropoietin receptor (EPOR) mediated signaling are essential for erythropoiesis.
claims.source: Both stem cell factor receptor KIT and erythropoietin receptor (EPOR) mediated signaling are essential for erythropoiesis.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claims.claim: CCND3 fills a critical role in regulating the number of cell divisions during terminal erythropoiesis.
claims.source: CCND3 fills a critical role in regulating the number of cell divisions during terminal erythropoiesis and has been validated as a causal gene associated with variation in RBC counts and size (Sankaran et al., 2012; Ulirsch et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claims.claim: SLC4A1, also known as band 3, serves as a key component of the RBC membrane skeleton.
claims.source: Our method recovered characteristic RBC genes like solute carrier family 4 member 1 (SLC4A1), also known as band 3, (Peters et al., 1996), which serves as a key component of the RBC membrane skeleton.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a published study.

claims.claim: Ankyrin 1 (ANK1) is a direct interacting partner for SLC4A1 which anchors the cytoskeleton and cell membrane.
claims.source: Likewise, it recovered a direct interacting partner for SLC4A1, ankyrin 1 (ANK1), which anchors the cytoskeleton and cell membrane (Bennett and Stenbuck, 1979)
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a published study.

claims.claim: N-ethylmaleimide Sensitive Factor (NSF) facilitates membrane vesicle trafficking within the cell.
claims.source: as well as N-ethylmaleimide Sensitive Factor, vesicle fusing ATPase (NSF), which facilitates membrane vesicle trafficking within the cell (Glick and Rothman, 1987).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a published study.

claims.claim: RPL7A and RPL19 have been implicated by mutations observed in studies of Diamond-Blackfan anemia.
claims.source: Both RPL7A and RPL19, for instance, have been implicated by mutations observed in studies of Diamond-Blackfan anemia (Gazda et al., 2012; DBA Group of Société d'Hématologie et d'Immunologie Pédiatrique-SHIP et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claims.claim: Common genetic variation affecting ribosomal protein genes might contribute to the incomplete penetrance and variable expressivity of anemia seen in Diamond-Blackfan anemia patients.
claims.source: The common genetic variation affecting these ribosomal protein genes might contribute to the incomplete penetrance and variable expressivity of anemia seen in Diamond-Blackfan anemia patients (Ulirsch et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citation.

claims.claim: Common genetic variants may influence phenotypic outcomes in patients with neurodevelopmental disorders.
claims.source: Similar effects have been reported in neurodevelopmental disorders, where common genetic variants may influence phenotypic outcomes in patients (Niemi et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a published study.

claims.claim: Exosome component 9 (EXOSC9) has been suggested to act as part of the exosome complex as a specific gatekeeper of terminal erythroid maturation.
claims.source: Exosome component 9 (EXOSC9), for instance, has been suggested to act as part of the exosome complex as a specific gatekeeper of terminal erythroid maturation (McIver et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a published study.

claims.claim: TFR2 encodes a protein canonically involved in iron homeostasis that has recently been shown to also regulate EPO receptor signaling.
claims.source: The first, transferrin receptor 2 (TFR2), encodes a protein canonically involved in iron homeostasis that has recently been shown to also regulate EPO receptor signaling (Forejtnikovà et al., 2010; Nai et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claims.claim: TFR2 has been studied in the context of murine erythropoiesis, but its role in human erythropoiesis has not been assessed.
claims.source: Although TFR2 has been studied in the context of murine erythropoiesis, its role in human erythropoiesis has not been assessed.
claims.evidence: This identifies a gap in the literature.

claims.claim: Significant knockdown of TFR2 was observed at both the mRNA and protein levels using two independent shRNAs.
claims.source: Significant knockdown of TFR2 was observed at both the mRNA (Figure 5A) and protein levels (Figure 5B) using two independent shRNAs from among the six targeting TFR2 in the screen.
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in figures.

claims.claim: Downregulation of TFR2 increased erythroid differentiation as observed by increased expression of erythroid-specific cell surface markers CD235a and CD71 at day 9 and day 12 of culture.
claims.source: Downregulation of TFR2 increased erythroid differentiation as observed by increased expression of erythroid-specific cell surface markers CD235a and CD71 at day 9 (shLUC ~22%; TFR2 sh1 ~42%; TFR2 sh2 ~40%) and day 12 of culture (shLUC ~60%; TF2 sh1 ~80%; TFR2 sh2 ~80%) (Figure 5C and E).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in figures.

claims.claim: Downregulation of TFR2 improved the later stages of erythroid differentiation/maturation, as observed by loss of cell surface marker CD49d at day 15 of culture, an increased rate of enucleation, and through assessment of cell morphology.
claims.source: Downregulation of TFR2 also improved the later stages of erythroid differentiation/maturation, as observed by loss of cell surface marker CD49d at day 15 of culture, an increased rate of enucleation, and through assessment of cell morphology (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in figures.

claims.claim: TFR2 has been isolated as a component of the erythropoietin (EPO) receptor complex.
claims.source: Previous studies have reported the isolation of TFR2 as a component of the erythropoietin (EPO) receptor complex (Forejtnikovà et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a published study.

claims.claim: TFR2 downregulation resulted in significantly higher pSTAT5 phosphorylation in comparison to the control with EPO stimulation from 0.02 U/mL to 200 U/mL.
claims.source: TFR2 downregulation resulted in significantly higher pSTAT5 phosphorylation in comparison to the control with EPO stimulation from 0.02 U/mL to 200 U/mL (Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in a figure.

claims.claim: The maximal pSTAT5 response could be achieved within a shorter period of EPO stimulation upon TFR2 downregulation.
claims.source: In addition, the maximal pSTAT5 response could be achieved within a shorter period of EPO stimulation upon TFR2 downregulation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in a figure.

claims.claim: TFR2 is a negative regulator of EPO signaling.
claims.source: Given our findings that TFR2 is a negative regulator of EPO signaling, it may be an ideal therapeutic target for conditions characterized by ineffective erythropoiesis like β-thalassemia (Rund and Rachmilewitz, 2005).
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data, with citation to background on β-thalassemia.

claims.claim: Tfr2 downregulation is beneficial in a mouse model of β-thalassemia.
claims.source: A recent study has supported this hypothesis, showing that Tfr2 downregulation is beneficial in a mouse model of β-thalassemia (Artuso et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a published study.

claims.claim: Extensive mRNA splicing occurs during the terminal stages of erythropoiesis.
claims.source: Extensive mRNA splicing occurs during the terminal stages of erythropoiesis (Pimentel et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a published study.

claims.claim: SF3A2 is a component of the U2SNRP complex whose binding to the branch point is critical for proper mRNA splicing.
claims.source: SF3A2 is a component of the U2SNRP complex whose binding to the branch point is critical for proper mRNA splicing (Gozani et al., 1996; Gozani et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claims.claim: SF3A2 was associated with maximal hairpin drop out at day 12 (FDR = 0.005).
claims.source: SF3A2 specifically was associated with maximal hairpin drop out at day 12 (FDR = 0.005) – a later time point in erythropoiesis.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the screen results.

claims.claim: Knockdown of SF3A2 in primary human CD34+ HSPCs results in decreased cell numbers during erythroid differentiation starting from day 7.
claims.source: Knockdown of SF3A2 in primary human CD34+ HSPCs results in decreased cell numbers during erythroid differentiation starting from day 7 (Figure 6A–C).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in figures.

claims.claim: Decreased cell numbers were associated with decreased erythroid differentiation as measured by erythroid surface markers CD71 and CD235a.
claims.source: Decreased cell numbers were associated with decreased erythroid differentiation as measured by erythroid surface markers CD71 and CD235a (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in a figure.

claims.claim: An increase in non-erythroid lineages based on surface marker expression of CD11b (myeloid) and CD41a (megakaryocytic) was observed upon SF3A2 knockdown.
claims.source: We also observed an increase in non-erythroid lineages based on surface marker expression of CD11b (myeloid) and CD41a (megakaryocytic) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in a figure.

claims.claim: Cells treated with shRNA to suppress SF3A2 were found to differentially express 6061 genes with an adjusted p value < 0.05 as compared to the shLuc control.
claims.source: Cells treated with shRNA to suppress SF3A2 were found to differentially express 6061 genes with an adjusted p value < 0.05 as compared to the shLuc control
claims.evidence: This is a finding from RNA-seq analysis.

claims.claim: Only 807 genes were differentially expressed in MDS patients with SF3B1 mutations compared to those without.
claims.source: whereas only 807 genes were differentially expressed given the same threshold cutoff in the MDS patients with an SF3B1 mutations compared to those without (Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from RNA-seq analysis of MDS patient data.

claims.claim: Genes from both the SF3A2 differentially expressed set and the SF3B1 differentially expressed set were significantly enriched for structural constituents of the ribosome.
claims.source: Genes from both the SF3A2 differentially expressed set and the SF3B1 differentially expressed set were significantly enriched for structural constituents of the ribosome (p<3.2×10−44 and p<7.5×10-24, respectively) among other cellular components and functions (Figure 6—source data 3 and 4).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from pathway enrichment analysis.

claims.claim: Both SF3A2 and SF3B1 knockdown were found to exhibit a similar proportion of altered splicing events.
claims.source: Examining differential splicing in the set of genes not differentially expressed in either condition, both were found to exhibit a similar proportion of altered splicing events, including alternative 3' splice sites, alternative 5' splice sites, mutually exclusive exons, and skipped exons (Figure 6E).

results.result: A pooled shRNA screen was designed to interrogate 389 candidate genes from 75 GWAS loci associated with red blood cell traits, identifying 77 genes at 38 loci, with most loci harboring 1-2 candidate genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C5 and C15-C20 describe the experimental design and primary outcome of the screen. The methodology for gene selection using LD blocks and gene wingspan is clearly described (C17-C18), resulting in 389 genes (C19-C20). The screen successfully identified 77 genes at 38 loci (C4), with most loci having 1-2 genes (C5), which is well-documented in the data.

results.result: The 77 identified genes were validated through multiple orthogonal approaches, showing significant enrichment for erythroid essentiality, known 'gold standard' genes, and fine-mapped coding variants.
results.evaluation: Claims C6 and C47-C53 present comprehensive validation analyses with statistical support. The hit set showed enrichment for K562 essentiality (p=0.0269, C47), genome-wide essentiality (p=0.00021, C48), lipid GWAS comparisons (C49), five gold standard genes (p=0.0249, C51), and coding variants (p=0.03907, C53). These multiple independent validation approaches strongly support the quality of the identified genes.

results.result: The identified genes are enriched in relevant biological pathways and cell types, including signaling/transcription, membrane structure, and mRNA translation, with expression enriched in erythroid progenitor stages.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C54-C55, C58-C59, and C101 describe pathway and expression analyses. The genes showed significant enrichment in CMPs and MEPs (p<0.01, C54) and specific erythroblast stages (p<0.001, C55). STRING network analysis identified relevant biological processes (C58-C59). These findings are well-supported by the data and figures presented.

results.result: shRNA-based screening was chosen over CRISPR approaches due to superior efficiency in primary HSPCs, avoidance of unpredictable DNA repair outcomes, and better recapitulation of subtle gene expression changes characteristic of common genetic variation.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C28 justify the methodological choice of shRNA over CRISPR. The rationale is supported by citations (C24-C25, C27-C28) and experimental data showing low titer issues with CRISPR constructs (C26). The arguments are logical and well-documented, though the comparison relies partly on cited literature rather than direct head-to-head experiments in this study.

results.result: The experimental design used a pooled shRNA library with 2803 hairpins (5-7 per gene) infecting at least 1000 CD34+ HSPCs per hairpin, achieving 35-50% infectivity, with genomic DNA sequenced at six time points during erythroid differentiation.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C34 describe the experimental execution. The library composition (C29-C30), infection parameters (C31-C32), and sampling strategy (C34) are clearly documented. The hypothesis (C33) is reasonable based on cited prior work. These methodological details are well-supported and appropriate for the experimental goals.

results.result: The screen showed high library representation (>95% of hairpins at ≥5 log2 CPM at day 4) with diverse effects across the time course, including expected depletion of hairpins targeting known erythroid genes (GATA1, RPS19) and essential genes, with strong correlation across three donor replicates.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C39 describe quality control metrics and positive controls. The high representation (C35), diverse effects (C36), and expected behavior of controls (C37-C38) demonstrate technical success. Strong correlation across donors (C39) supports reproducibility. These are well-documented in the figures and represent solid experimental validation.

results.result: A linear mixed model accounting for longitudinal data and shRNA off-target effects identified 77 genes at 38 loci using thresholds of β>0.1 log2 fold change per day and FDR q<0.1, with 27 loci having 1-2 gene targets and hits distributed across all 6 RBC traits showing strong internal consistency.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C46 describe the statistical analysis and results. The linear mixed model approach (C40) with appropriate data transformation (C41) and dual thresholds (C42) is methodologically sound and supported by citations. The results (C43-C46) are clearly presented with good internal consistency. The statistical framework appropriately addresses the experimental design.

results.result: The shRNA screen hits did not overlap with genes identified by eQTLs from GTEx whole blood, likely because the screen was performed on differentiating erythroid progenitors not present in whole blood, emphasizing cell-type specificity.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C57 and C102-C103 describe the comparison with eQTL data. The lack of overlap (C56, C102) is documented, and the explanation based on cell-type differences (C57, C103) is logical and well-reasoned. This finding highlights the complementary nature of the approach and is appropriately interpreted.

results.result: TFR2 was validated as a negative regulator of human erythropoiesis, with knockdown increasing erythroid differentiation, enhancing EPO-dependent STAT5 phosphorylation, and improving terminal maturation.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C80 present comprehensive validation of TFR2. The knockdown is confirmed at mRNA and protein levels (C74), with clear phenotypic effects on differentiation (C75-C76) and EPO signaling (C78-C79). The data are shown in multiple figures with quantification. The conclusion that TFR2 is a negative regulator (C80) is well-supported by the experimental evidence, though the therapeutic speculation is appropriately cautious.

results.result: SF3A2, a component of the U2SNRP splicing complex, was identified as a regulator of erythropoiesis, with knockdown causing decreased cell numbers, reduced erythroid differentiation, and increased non-erythroid lineages.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C87 establish SF3A2's role in erythropoiesis. The background on splicing (C82-C83) is well-cited, the screen result is clear (C84), and the validation experiments (C85-C87) show consistent phenotypes with multiple shRNAs and controls. The data are presented in figures with appropriate quantification.

results.result: RNA-seq analysis of SF3A2 knockdown showed differential expression of 6061 genes and altered splicing patterns similar to SF3B1 mutant MDS patients, with both conditions enriched for ribosomal genes and exhibiting similar proportions of altered splicing events.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C91 present RNA-seq findings comparing SF3A2 knockdown to SF3B1 mutations. The differential expression (C88-C89), pathway enrichment (C90), and splicing analysis (C91) are clearly documented. The comparison to MDS patient data provides important biological context and is appropriately analyzed.

results.result: In a mouse model of MDS with Sf3b1K700E mutation, Sf3a2 knockdown further worsened the defects in erythroid differentiation and cell growth, suggesting SF3A2 modulates SF3B1-driven MDS phenotypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C94 describe genetic interaction experiments in a mouse MDS model. The baseline phenotype (C92) and worsening with Sf3a2 knockdown (C93) are clearly shown in figures. The conclusion about disease modification (C94) is appropriately stated as a suggestion based on the data. The experiments provide strong evidence for genetic interaction.

results.result: A coding SNP (rs25672) in SF3A2 was identified in LD with the sentinel SNP (r2=0.737675), and MDS patients with SF3B1 mutations show variable anemia severity at presentation.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C96 describe genetic findings related to SF3A2 and MDS. The identification of the coding variant (C96) is straightforward genetic analysis. The clinical variability in MDS (C95) is supported by citation. These provide context for potential disease modification, though the connection is not definitively established in this study.

results.result: The LD-based gene selection approach has limitations, potentially missing genes targeted by long-range regulatory interactions, as LD metrics only nominate a fraction of potential regulatory targets.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C22 and C108 acknowledge methodological limitations. These are appropriately cited (C21-C22, C108) and represent honest assessment of the approach's boundaries. The acknowledgment of limitations is important for proper interpretation of the results.

results.result: The gene-centric screening approach requires suitable model systems and faces challenges from shRNA off-target effects, though appropriate controls and modeling can address these issues.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C107 discuss limitations and considerations for the approach. The need for suitable systems (C105) and shRNA off-target concerns (C106) are valid limitations. The mitigation strategies (C107) are appropriately cited. This represents balanced discussion of the method's applicability and constraints.

results.result: The screen successfully identified 77 genes at 38 loci with strong erythroid essentiality, including known gold standard genes and enrichment for coding variants, demonstrating that gene-centric screens are valuable for GWAS follow-up.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C100 and C109 summarize the main findings and conclusions. The results (C97-C100) are well-supported by the data presented throughout. The conclusion about the value of gene-centric screens (C109) is justified by the successful identification and validation of genes. This represents an appropriate synthesis of the work.

results.result: Network analysis identified known regulators of erythropoiesis including transcription factors (MYB, ETO2), signaling molecules (KIT, EPOR, CCND3), membrane proteins (SLC4A1, ANK1, NSF), and ribosomal proteins (RPL7A, RPL19) implicated in Diamond-Blackfan anemia.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C71 describe known genes identified in the screen with extensive literature support. Each gene's role is appropriately cited (C60-C68, C71). The speculation about common variants affecting DBA penetrance (C69-C70) is appropriately tentative and cited. This demonstrates the screen's ability to recover known biology while providing context for novel findings.

results.result: A recent study showed that Tfr2 downregulation is beneficial in a mouse model of β-thalassemia, supporting the therapeutic potential of targeting TFR2.
results.evaluation: Claim C81 cites external validation of the TFR2 findings in a disease model. This is appropriately cited and provides important context for the therapeutic relevance of the findings, though it represents work from another group rather than data from this study.

results.result: SF3A2 and potentially other regulators like mRNA translation factors may be key disease modifiers that alter impaired erythropoiesis in MDS or Diamond-Blackfan anemia.
results.evaluation: Claim C104 is a hypothesis based on the experimental findings. While the SF3A2 data in the MDS model (C92-C94) provide some support, the extension to other regulators and to Diamond-Blackfan anemia is speculative. The claim is appropriately tentative ('may be') but requires additional validation beyond what is presented.

results.result: Gene-centric screens are not limited to red cell traits and may be useful for other human traits/diseases, with data potentially integrated with variant-centric screens.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C111 propose broader applications of the approach. While C110 cites one example in type 2 diabetes, the generalizability to other traits/diseases and the integration with variant-centric screens (C111) remain to be demonstrated. These are reasonable future directions but are not directly supported by the current work.
